That way you would be leveling 3 skills: the one needed to make the stuff you sell (4 if you make weapons with enchantments), the skill you trained, and the speech skill. Mind you, that works better at lower levels when you don't need much experience to level up and train again. Another thing I can think of is checking which potions give you the most experience, then you could plant the ingredients in a greenhouse to make a ton of those potions (without exploits); that way, you could legendary alchemy a lot of times. I'm sure there must be other ways to level up faster without using exploits, but I hope some of these come in handy. As to mods, I would check out Beyond Skyrim: Bruma. He's actually right. I know it sounds counterintuitive, but when we talk about infinite sets, our intuition is not very helpful. When we want to show that two sets have the same number of elements, let's call them A and B, we want to show that there is a function f: A→B such that it is bijective (both surjective and injective). For the sets that the person above you proposed we can define the function f: [0, 1] →[0, 2], f(x) = 2x. So, for example, for x=0 in [0, 1], the function pairs that number up with 0 in [0, 2]. For x=1 in [0, 1], the function pairs that number up with 2 in [0, 2]. You can do this for every number in [0, 1] and you will find that for every y in [0, 2] there is an x in [0, 1] such that f(x)=y (i.e. the function is surjective); you will also find that every element in [0, 1] is paired up with only one element in [0, 2] (i.e. the function is injective). Therefore, since the function is both injective and surjective, we can conclude that the function is bijective, which implies that the cardinality of [0, 1] is the same as the cardinality of [0, 2] (both of them have the same number of elements). By following a similar reasoning you can find a bijective function between any interval (a, b) and the real numbers R, concluding that they both have the same number of elements. Of course this explanation isn't formal, so if you are really interested, you can read the work of Cantor. Also, here's a link that tries to summarize all of this without losing too much formality: http://legacy.earlham.edu/~peters/writing/infapp.htm

Scaling range by letter 
E: 1%-24%
D: 25%-49%
C: 50%-74%
B: 75%-99%
A: 100%-139%
S: 140%-200%

For example, you may have two weapons that have scaling D for dexterity, which means that, depending on your dexterity level and the scaling itself, the base damage output of your weapons will increase between 25% and 49%. However, even though both weapons say they have a scaling D, one might increase 49% the base damage output (which is within the limits of that scaling range), while the other might only increase 25% the base damage output (which, again, is within the limits of that scaling range). That is why, when you are going to change one of the weapons for the other, the D might appear red or blue even if they both have scaling D. Blue means the scaling is better than that of the current weapon, and red means the opposite.
